abstract: Trinity Health, a major US health system operating 92 hospitals across 15 states, announced a 10.5% reduction in its revenue cycle management workforce in January 2026. The layoffs are part of a broader effort to manage rising costs, low payer reimbursement, staffing shortages, and anticipated Medicaid cuts. Non-patient-facing revenue cycle functions will be transitioned to an external partner, reflecting the industry trend toward AI and automation in administrative healthcare roles.
keyFindings: 10.5% of revenue cycle management staff laid off across Trinity Health's national footprint of 92 hospitals in 15 states
Non-patient-facing revenue cycle functions transitioned to an external partner
Trinity Health reported $12.2M operating loss on $25.4B revenue in FY2025 (ending June 30, 2025)
System incurred $13.6B in labor costs (up from $12.9B in FY2024) and spent $50.4M on severance and termination benefits
Anticipated Medicaid cuts could cost the system up to $1.1B across its 92 hospitals
methodology: Corporate disclosure reported across Healthcare Dive, Modern Healthcare, Becker's Hospital Review, and other outlets. Financial data from Trinity Health's FY2025 earnings report.
qualifiers: The layoffs were attributed to multiple financial pressures (low reimbursement, supply costs, staffing shortages, federal funding cuts), not solely to AI or automation. The outsourcing to an external partner aligns with the broader industry trend of AI-driven revenue cycle management, but Trinity Health did not explicitly cite AI as the primary driver. Industry analysts note that revenue cycle has been the area most able to capitalize on AI technologies given its transactional nature.
